We study the limiting eigenvalue distribution of $n\times n$ banded Toeplitz matrices as $n\to \infty$. From classical results of Schmidt-Spitzer and Hirschman it is known that the eigenvalues accumulate on a special curve in the complex plane and the normalized eigenvalue counting measure converges weakly to a measure on this curve as $n\to\infty$. In this paper, we characterize the limiting measure in terms of an equilibrium problem. The limiting measure is one component of the unique vector of measures that minimes an energy functional defined on admissible vectors of measures. In addition, we show that each of the other components is the limiting measure of the normalized counting measure on certain generalized eigenvalues.

outputs.L1: We study the limiting eigenvalue distribution of \(n \times n\) banded Toeplitz matrices as \(n \to \infty\). Classical results of Schmidt–Spitzer and Hirschman establish that the eigenvalues accumulate on a distinguished curve in the complex plane and that the normalized eigenvalue counting measure converges weakly to a measure supported on this curve. In this paper, we characterize the limiting measure in terms of an equilibrium problem. Specifically, the limiting measure is one component of the unique vector of measures that minimizes an energy functional defined on the class of admissible vectors of measures. In addition, we show that each of the remaining components arises as the limiting normalized counting measure of certain generalized eigenvalues.
outputs.L2: We investigate the asymptotic spectral behavior of \(n\times n\) banded Toeplitz matrices as \(n\) tends to infinity. Classical theorems due to Schmidt–Spitzer and Hirschman establish that their eigenvalues concentrate along a distinguished curve in the complex plane, while the associated normalized eigenvalue-counting measures converge weakly to a measure supported on that curve. We describe this limiting measure through an equilibrium problem: it appears as one entry of the unique admissible vector of measures minimizing a specified energy functional. We further prove that every remaining entry of this vector arises as the limit of normalized counting measures for suitable generalized eigenvalues.
outputs.L3:
The paper investigates the asymptotic eigenvalue distribution of \(n \times n\) banded Toeplitz matrices as the matrix size \(n\) tends to infinity. Classical results establish that, in this limit, the eigenvalues accumulate on a distinguished curve in the complex plane. More precisely, the normalized eigenvalue counting measures converge weakly to a probability measure supported on this limiting curve.

The principal contribution of the paper is a potential-theoretic characterization of this limiting measure. It is identified as one component of a unique vector of measures that minimizes an associated energy functional in a vector equilibrium problem. The remaining components of the minimizing vector also have a spectral interpretation: they arise as the limiting normalized counting measures of certain generalized eigenvalues related to the Toeplitz matrices. Thus, the equilibrium problem provides a unified framework for describing both the ordinary eigenvalue distribution and the asymptotic distributions of these generalized spectral quantities.
outputs.L4:
Let  
\[
a(z)=\sum_{j=-q}^{p}a_jz^j,\qquad a_{-q}a_p\neq 0,
\]
be a Laurent polynomial, and let \(T_n(a)\) denote the \(n\times n\) banded Toeplitz matrix generated by \(a\). The entries of \(T_n(a)\) are constant along diagonals, with  
\[
(T_n(a))_{jk}=a_{j-k}.
\]
The problem is to determine the asymptotic distribution of the eigenvalues of \(T_n(a)\) as \(n\to\infty\). Although Toeplitz matrices are defined by a simple symbol, their eigenvalues need not lie on the image \(a(\mathbb T)\) of the unit circle, particularly when the matrices are non-Hermitian. Their limiting behavior is instead governed by a system of algebraic curves and an associated vector equilibrium problem.

For a fixed complex number \(\lambda\), consider the equation  
\[
a(z)=\lambda.
\]
After multiplication by \(z^q\), this becomes a polynomial equation of degree \(p+q\). Denote its roots, counted with multiplicity, by  
\[
z_1(\lambda),\ldots,z_{p+q}(\lambda),
\]
ordered so that  
\[
|z_1(\lambda)|\leq \cdots\leq |z_{p+q}(\lambda)|.
\]
The relevant curves in the \(\lambda\)-plane are defined by equality of two consecutive root moduli:
\[
\Gamma_k=\left\{\lambda\in\mathbb C:
|z_{q+k}(\lambda)|=|z_{q+k+1}(\lambda)|\right\},
\qquad -q+1\leq k\leq p-1.
\]
In particular, \(\Gamma_0\) is the classical limiting spectral curve for the eigenvalues of \(T_n(a)\). Under the usual nondegeneracy assumptions, the normalized eigenvalue counting measures
\[
\nu_n=\frac1n\sum_{\lambda\in \operatorname{spec}(T_n(a))}
\delta_\lambda
\]
converge weakly to a measure \(\mu_0\) supported on \(\Gamma_0\).

The measure \(\mu_0\) is most naturally understood as one component of a larger vector of measures
\[
\boldsymbol{\mu}
=(\mu_{-q+1},\ldots,\mu_{p-1}),
\]
where each \(\mu_k\) is supported on \(\Gamma_k\). The masses of these measures are prescribed by the position of the corresponding curve in the chain. In the standard normalization,
\[
\mu_k(\Gamma_k)=
\begin{cases}
1+\dfrac{k}{q}, & -q+1\leq k\leq 0,\\[6pt]
1-\dfrac{k}{p}, & 0\leq k\leq p-1.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus \(\mu_0\) has total mass one and is therefore the limiting probability measure for the ordinary eigenvalues.

The vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) is characterized as the unique minimizer of a logarithmic energy functional. For finite measures \(\sigma\) and \(\tau\), write
\[
I(\sigma,\tau)
=\iint \log\frac1{|x-y|}\,d\sigma(x)\,d\tau(y),
\qquad
I(\sigma)=I(\sigma,\sigma).
\]
The equilibrium energy has the form
\[
J(\boldsymbol{\mu})
=
\sum_{k=-q+1}^{p-1} I(\mu_k)
-
\sum_{k=-q+1}^{p-2} I(\mu_k,\mu_{k+1}),
\]
possibly supplemented by external-field terms in degenerate or modified settings. Each measure repels itself logarithmically, while neighboring components attract one another. Components whose indices differ by more than one do not interact directly. Equivalently, the interaction is described by a tridiagonal positive-definite matrix with diagonal entries \(1\) and neighboring off-diagonal entries \(-\tfrac12\).

The admissible class consists of vectors of positive measures satisfying the support and mass restrictions above and having finite logarithmic energy. The strict convexity of the interaction functional yields uniqueness of the minimizing vector. Its components satisfy coupled Euler–Lagrange conditions. On the support of \(\mu_k\), the effective potential
\[
2U^{\mu_k}(x)-U^{\mu_{k-1}}(x)-U^{\mu_{k+1}}(x),
\qquad
U^\sigma(x)=\int\log\frac1{|x-y|}\,d\sigma(y),
\]
is constant, with the evident modifications at the two ends of the chain. Away from the support, the corresponding variational inequality holds. These conditions connect the potential-theoretic minimizer with the algebraic definition of the curves \(\Gamma_k\).

The first component of direct spectral interest is \(\mu_0\). It describes the limiting distribution of the zeros of
\[
\det\!\left(T_n(a)-\lambda I\right),
\]
and hence of the eigenvalues of the original Toeplitz matrices. The remaining components are not merely auxiliary measures introduced to formulate the equilibrium problem. They also possess a spectral interpretation.

For each admissible index \(k\), one considers the generalized characteristic determinant
\[
P_{k,n}(\lambda)
=
\det T_n\!\left(z^{-k}(a(z)-\lambda)\right).
\]
When \(k=0\), this reduces to the ordinary characteristic polynomial, up to an inessential sign convention:
\[
P_{0,n}(\lambda)=\det(T_n(a)-\lambda I).
\]
For \(k\neq0\), the zeros of \(P_{k,n}\) may be viewed as generalized eigenvalues associated with shifted Toeplitz pencils. After normalization by their asymptotic degree, the zero counting measures of these determinants converge weakly to \(\mu_k\). Thus every component of the equilibrium vector arises as a limiting distribution of a natural family of generalized eigenvalues.

This result extends the usual spectral description in two ways. First, it replaces the study of a single limiting eigenvalue measure by a coupled system of measures supported on several algebraic curves. Second, it shows that the additional measures required by the equilibrium formulation have an intrinsic matrix-theoretic meaning. They are limits of normalized counting measures for generalized characteristic equations, rather than purely formal objects introduced by potential theory.

Consequently, the asymptotic spectral theory of large banded Toeplitz matrices is governed by a unified structure. The roots of the symbol equation determine the supporting curves, logarithmic potential theory determines the unique equilibrium vector, and Toeplitz determinants supply the spectral interpretation of all its components. The ordinary limiting eigenvalue distribution is precisely the central component \(\mu_0\), while the neighboring components encode the asymptotic zeros of related generalized eigenvalue problems.
outputs.L5:
### From Schmidt to Toeplitz

The names Erhard Schmidt and Otto Toeplitz are closely connected with the development of modern functional analysis. Schmidt is remembered for the Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization process and for his work on integral equations and Hilbert spaces. His ideas provided powerful methods for representing complicated functions through orthogonal systems.

Toeplitz, meanwhile, studied operators that can be represented by matrices whose entries are constant along each diagonal. These **Toeplitz matrices** now appear in signal processing, numerical analysis, probability, and time-series modeling.

From Schmidt’s orthogonal methods to Toeplitz’s structured operators, their work helped transform abstract mathematical concepts into practical tools. Their contributions continue to influence both theoretical research and modern computational applications.

This potential-theoretic formulation provides an explicit description of the limiting density, its support, and possible exceptional generalized eigenvalues.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main results of a paper that characterizes the limiting eigenvalue measure of \(n\times n\) banded Toeplitz matrices using a vector equilibrium problem.
counterfactuals.output:
For a Laurent polynomial symbol  
\[
a(z)=\sum_{j=-q}^{p}a_jz^j,\qquad a_{-q}a_p\neq0,
\]
let \(T_n(a)=(a_{j-k})_{j,k=1}^n\) be the associated banded Toeplitz matrix. The paper’s main results are:

- **Spectral curves from the symbol.** For each \(\lambda\), order the \(p+q\) solutions of
  \[
  a(z)=\lambda
  \]
  by modulus, \(|z_1(\lambda)|\le\cdots\le |z_{p+q}(\lambda)|\). It introduces curves
  \[
  \Gamma_k=\{\lambda:\ |z_{q+k}(\lambda)|=|z_{q+k+1}(\lambda)|\},
  \qquad -q+1\le k\le p-1.
  \]
  In particular, \(\Gamma_0\) is the limiting spectral set of the Toeplitz matrices.

- **Limiting eigenvalue distribution.** If
  \[
  \nu_n=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\delta_{\lambda_j(T_n(a))}
  \]
  is the normalized eigenvalue-counting measure, then
  \[
  \nu_n \xrightarrow[]{\,w\,}\mu_0,
  \]
  where \(\mu_0\) is a probability measure supported on \(\Gamma_0\). Thus the result refines the classical description of the limiting spectrum by determining how eigenvalues are distributed along it.

- **A full vector of measures.** Measures \(\mu_k\) are defined on all the curves \(\Gamma_k\), using jumps of the logarithmic derivatives of the ordered roots across those curves. Formally, their densities are of the type
  \[
  d\mu_k(\lambda)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}
  \sum_{j=1}^{q+k}
  \left(\frac{z'_{j,+}}{z_{j,+}}-
        \frac{z'_{j,-}}{z_{j,-}}\right)d\lambda .
  \]
  They are positive and have prescribed masses
  \[
  \mu_k(\Gamma_k)=
  \begin{cases}
  \dfrac{q+k}{q},&-q+1\le k\le0,\\[4pt]
  \dfrac{p-k}{p},&0\le k\le p-1.
  \end{cases}
  \]
  Hence \(\mu_0(\Gamma_0)=1\).

- **Vector equilibrium characterization.** The vector
  \[
  (\mu_{-q+1},\ldots,\mu_{p-1})
  \]
  is the unique minimizer, among measures with these supports and masses, of the logarithmic energy
  \[
  J(\boldsymbol{\nu})
  =\sum_{k=-q+1}^{p-1} I(\nu_k)
   -\sum_{k=-q+1}^{p-2}I(\nu_k,\nu_{k+1}),
  \]
  where
  \[
  I(\nu,\sigma)=\iint\log\frac1{|x-y|}\,d\nu(x)d\sigma(y).
  \]
  Thus each component repels itself logarithmically but is attracted to its nearest neighbors; non-neighboring components do not interact.

- **Equilibrium relations.** The minimizer satisfies Euler–Lagrange conditions of the form
  \[
  2U^{\mu_k}-U^{\mu_{k-1}}-U^{\mu_{k+1}}
  =\ell_k \quad\text{on }\Gamma_k,
  \]
  with the endpoint measures interpreted as zero. These identities connect the potential-theoretic equilibrium directly to the algebraic functions \(z_j(\lambda)\).

The conceptual contribution is that the limiting eigenvalue law \(\mu_0\), previously described through root-modulus conditions, becomes one component of a canonical and uniquely solvable vector equilibrium problem. This provides a potential-theoretic framework that also clarifies positivity, support, masses, and the interaction among the different spectral curves.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a mathematical abstract explaining how the Schmidt–Spitzer and Hirschman results are extended by interpreting the limiting spectral measure and related generalized eigenvalue measures as components of an energy-minimizing vector of measures.
counterfactuals.output: We extend the classical results of Schmidt–Spitzer and Hirschman on the asymptotic eigenvalue distribution of banded Toeplitz matrices. For a Laurent-polynomial symbol, Schmidt–Spitzer identified the limiting spectral set through the equimodularity of consecutive roots of the associated algebraic equation, while Hirschman obtained the corresponding limiting eigenvalue measure. We show that this measure belongs to a natural family of measures supported on the equimodular curves determined by the ordered roots of the symbol equation. These measures, which arise as limiting zero distributions of suitable generalized eigenvalue determinants, form the components of a vector equilibrium problem with logarithmic interactions of nearest-neighbor type and externally imposed masses. The resulting vector of measures is characterized uniquely as the minimizer of an energy functional, and its distinguished central component is precisely the limiting spectral measure of the Toeplitz matrices. This variational interpretation recovers the Schmidt–Spitzer limiting spectrum and Hirschman’s measure while placing them in a broader potential-theoretic framework that simultaneously describes the asymptotics of generalized eigenvalues.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a brief academic overview of the asymptotic eigenvalue distribution of large banded Toeplitz matrices, including weak convergence, accumulation on a complex curve, and the variational characterization of the limiting measure.
counterfactuals.output:
Let  
\[
a(z)=\sum_{k=-q}^{p}a_k z^k,\qquad a_{-q}a_p\neq0,
\]
and let \(T_n(a)=(a_{j-k})_{j,k=1}^n\) be the corresponding \(n\times n\) banded Toeplitz matrix. For each \(\lambda\in\mathbb C\), order the \(p+q\) roots of
\[
z^q(a(z)-\lambda)=0
\]
by modulus,
\[
|z_1(\lambda)|\leq\cdots\leq |z_{p+q}(\lambda)|.
\]

The Schmidt–Spitzer theory identifies the limiting spectral set as
\[
\Gamma=\{\lambda\in\mathbb C:\ |z_q(\lambda)|=|z_{q+1}(\lambda)|\}.
\]
Generically, \(\Gamma\) is a finite union of analytic arcs joined at branch points. Apart from possible exceptional eigenvalues of asymptotically negligible multiplicity, the eigenvalues of \(T_n(a)\) accumulate on \(\Gamma\).

If
\[
\mu_n=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\delta_{\lambda_j(T_n(a))}
\]
is the normalized eigenvalue-counting measure, then, under the usual nondegeneracy assumptions,
\[
\mu_n \xrightarrow{\mathrm{w}} \mu_0,
\]
where \(\mu_0\) is a probability measure supported on \(\Gamma\). On a regular oriented arc, its density can be expressed through the boundary values of the competing root \(z_q\):
\[
d\mu_0(\lambda)
 =\frac{1}{2\pi i}
 \left(
 \frac{z'_{q,+}(\lambda)}{z_{q,+}(\lambda)}
 -
 \frac{z'_{q,-}(\lambda)}{z_{q,-}(\lambda)}
 \right)d\lambda,
\]
with orientation chosen so that the measure is positive.

Equivalently, \(\mu_0\) is determined by its logarithmic potential:
\[
\int_\Gamma \log|\lambda-x|\,d\mu_0(x)
=
\log|a_p|+\sum_{j=q+1}^{p+q}\log|z_j(\lambda)|,
\qquad \lambda\notin\Gamma.
\]
This also yields a variational description. Writing
\[
V(\lambda)=\log|a_p|+\sum_{j=q+1}^{p+q}\log|z_j(\lambda)|,
\]
the measure \(\mu_0\) is the weighted logarithmic equilibrium measure on \(\Gamma\): it uniquely minimizes
\[
I_V(\nu)
=
\iint \log\frac1{|x-y|}\,d\nu(x)d\nu(y)
+2\int_\Gamma V(x)\,d\nu(x)
\]
over probability measures \(\nu\) supported on \(\Gamma\), with the associated Euler–Lagrange condition \(U^{\mu_0}+V=\text{constant}\) on the support. Thus the non-Hermitian spectral limit is governed jointly by root-modulus competition, logarithmic potential theory, and a weighted equilibrium principle.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output: **Abstract.** We study the asymptotic spectral distribution of finite \(n\times n\) Toeplitz matrices generated by a fixed symbol as \(n\to\infty\). After normalization by matrix size, the eigenvalue counting measures are shown to converge weakly to an equilibrium measure supported on the limiting spectral set determined by the symbol. This measure describes the bulk distribution of eigenvalues through the associated logarithmic-potential problem. The remaining components of the limiting spectral data arise as weak limits of normalized counting measures of generalized eigenvalues associated with the relevant Toeplitz pencils and boundary conditions. Our results provide a unified potential-theoretic description of both the principal spectral distribution and its residual components.
